Title: A Security Analysis of the OpenClaw AI Agent Framework
Abstract: AI agent frameworks that connect large language model (LLM) reasoning to real execution surfaces—shell, filesystem, containers, browser automation, and messaging platforms—introduce a class of security problems that differs structurally from conventional software. We study this through a systematic analysis of 470 security advisories filed against OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent runtime.We organize vulnerabilities along two independent axes: architectural layer, which captures where a vulnerability occurs, and adversarial technique, which captures how it is exploited. We further introduce a six-stage kill chain for personal AI agent systems, extending existing intrusion models with a Context Manipulation stage to capture attacks that subvert the LLM reasoning layer without triggering runtime policy checks. To ground the taxonomy, we analyze case studies across four architectural layers—the Plugin and Skill System, Agent Context Window, Tool Dispatch Interface, and Inter-Agent Communication surface—showing how vulnerabilities compose across layers.Across the corpus, the Gateway WebSocket Interface (25.7%) and Channel Input Interface (25.3%) together account for over half of all advisories, with moderate weaknesses composing into full host compromise. These patterns reflect two recurring root causes: brittle closed-world assumptions about input trustworthiness, and trust enforcement scattered across individual call sites rather than concentrated at inter-layer boundaries. Securing AI agent frameworks therefore requires unified policy enforcement at trust boundaries, rather than per-layer patching.
Major_Contribution_Result: The paper presents a systematic security analysis of the OpenClaw AI agent framework based on 470 security advisories, organizing them along architectural layer and adversarial technique axes and introducing a six-stage kill chain that adds a Context Manipulation stage. Across the corpus, the Gateway WebSocket Interface (25.7%) and Channel Input Interface (25.3%) together account for over half of advisories. Case studies illustrate composition of moderate weaknesses into host compromise (including a Gateway RCE chain) and a malicious skill that operates inside the LLM context to bypass the exec policy pipeline.

Critics: This is an advisory-corpus taxonomy and architectural case study of one open-source agent runtime rather than a controlled attack/defense benchmark. Security claims are grounded in GHSA-style evidence and patch differentials, which is strong for root-cause analysis but does not provide standardized ASR-style evaluation across models or frameworks. For LLM-agent security evaluation, the main transferable contribution is the two-axis taxonomy and kill-chain framing of cross-layer trust failures.
